title: Transcardial injection and vascular distribution of microalgae in Xenopus laevis as means to supply the brain with photosynthetic oxygen
protocol: Prepare a Styrofoam box with water at 17°C.
Insert a thermometer and maintain the ambient temperature at 17°C using ice or warm water.
Mount a tripod with a micromanipulator on a base plate next to the box.
Mount an O2-sensitive microsensor with tip diameter of 10 μm onto the micromanipulator for electrode advancement.
Suspend 0.1 or 0.5 × 10^9 cells/ml in 5 ml frog Ringer solution.
Fill the suspension into a tube with a diameter of 3 cm.
Place and firmly secure the tube containing the microalgae suspension inside the Styrofoam box.
Mount a tripod with an adjustable light source next to the Styrofoam box.
Place the end of the flexible fiber optics at a distance of 5 cm from the tube with sample.
Set the light intensity to 100 μE.
Insert the O2-sensitive microsensor into the suspension and maintain the algae for 30 min in darkness.
Illuminate the isolated algae suspension in the tube and record the gradual change in O2 concentration until a steady-state level is reached.
Prepare a circular dish by cleaning with 70% ethanol.
Mix Silicone Elastomer base (Sylgard) with curing agent at a ratio of 10:1 by gently stirring for 2–3 min.
Pour the viscous Sylgard compound into the circular dish up to a height of ∼3 mm.
Cover the dish to protect from dust.
Place the covered dish horizontally at 20°C for 1–2 days until the compound has become solid.
Pull microcapillaries on a horizontal puller using borosilicate glass (diameter: 1.5 mm, length 10 cm).
Break the tips of the pulled microcapillaries with fine forceps to reach an outer diameter of 50–100 μm.
Insert microcapillaries on a rotating grinder at an angle of 30° and gently grind the tip to obtain an injection needle-like sharp surface.
Make 5–6 microcapillaries for sufficient substitutes available for the injection.
Prepare a plain metal support plate of about 50 × 40 cm underneath a binocular with a zoomable lens.
Mount a tripod with a 3-axes micromanipulator on a base plate next to or on the main plate.
Attach an electrode holder equipped with a connector for applying pressurized air onto the micromanipulator.
Fix an incompressible polyethylene tube with an inner diameter of 2 mm to the electrode holder.
Connect the polyethylene tube to a pressure injection device.
Connect the pressure injection device with a BNC cable to an electrical pulse generator equipped with a remote control.
Adjust the pressure magnitude on the pressure injection device to 1 bar.
Set the pulse duration to 100 ms using the pulse generator.
Fill a container with crushed ice and place it underneath the binocular setup.
Place a fiber optics adjacent to the setup for illumination during surgery and injection.
Centrifuge cyanobacteria culture for 5 minutes at 3,000 g and 20°C to achieve a cell density of 10^10 cells/mL.
Resuspend the concentrated cyanobacteria in frog Ringer solution.
Centrifuge Chlamydomonas reinhardtii culture for 5 minutes between 150–290 g and 20°C to reach a cell density of 10^10 cells/mL.
Resuspend the concentrated C. reinhardtii in frog Ringer solution.
Enwrap the algae suspension container with aluminum foil to prevent light exposure.
Prepare an algal suspension sufficient for injection microcapillaries, typically 5 mL is adequate for easy handling and multiple refills.
Transcardially inject microalgae into Xenopus laevis tadpoles.
Dissolve 3-aminobenzoic acid ethyl ester methanesulfonate in a volume of 50 mL cold frog Ringer solution.
Store anesthetics at 4°C in darkness for up to two weeks.
Add PFA powder to 50 mL of 0.1 M phosphate buffer.
Gently stir the PFA solution on a heat plate at 62°C.
Add a few drops of 1 N NaOH to clear the solution completely.
Cool down the PFA fixative to 20°C.
Adjust pH with HCl to 7.3–7.4 before usage.
Place tadpole in 0.05% MS-222 solution until deeply anesthetized (lack of tail pinch-induced reflex).
Transfer anesthetized tadpole into Sylgard-lined circular dish filled with cold (∼10°C) frog Ringer solution and 0.05% MS-222.
Secure the anesthetized tadpole at the level of the rostral tail and head ventral side up with U-shaped pins to the floor of the Sylgard-lined dish.
Fill the container underneath the binocular with crushed ice to ensure continuous cooling of the frog Ringer solution during injection procedure.
Place and firmly fix the Sylgard-lined dish with the anesthetized and mechanically secured tadpole onto the flat surface above the container.
Use fiber optics to illuminate the preparation and optimize visibility of the tissue.
Gently remove skin above the heart with a microscissor and forceps, making the beating heart freely accessible.
Avoid excessive amounts of light to prevent light-stimulation of algae.
Open the container with concentrated suspension of microalgae.
Fill 10 μL of algae suspension into a long 20 μL tip without air bubbles.
Mix 8 μL algae suspension with 2 μL Isolectin GS-IB4 obtained from Griffonia simplicifolia Alexa FluorTM 488 conjugate.
Fill the solution bubble-free into the microcapillary.
Insert the microcapillary into the electrode holder mounted onto the 3-axes micromanipulator.
Advance the microcapillary until entering the Ringer solution above the tadpole and position the tip close to the surface of the beating heart.
Gently hold the beating heart steady with fine forceps.
Guide and insert the microcapillary with the 3-axes micromanipulator into the ventricular chamber of the heart.
Let the algae-filled microcapillary recover inside the heart for 1 min.
Manually trigger single pulses (100 ms, 1 bar) in synchrony with the heartbeat.
If no algae are injected, increase the pulse duration up to 200 ms and/or the pressure up to 2 bar.
If this is still unsuccessful, exchange the microcapillary for another one with a larger diameter.
Repeat (∼5 pulses per minute) until the volume of 10 μL has been injected; each pulse injects an approximate volume of 0.1–0.2 μL.
The injection of air into the heart with the last pulse must be avoided.
After the last pulse, gently remove the microcapillary.
Let the tadpole recover for 5 minutes before continuing the procedure.
Euthanize the animal after the recovery period.
Euthanize the tadpoles for anatomical visualization.
Extract the brain for imaging the vascular system and brain structure.
Free the deeply anesthetized tadpole from mechanical fixation.
Decapitate the animal with a small scissor at the level of the upper spinal cord.
Remove the lower jaws and visceral organs with the same scissor.
Pin the skull with the dorsal side up onto the Sylgard floor with minutiae.
Remove the skin of the skull with fine forceps and a microscissor.
Open the skull at the rostral end and remove the cartilaginous tissue above the brain until the decapitated end of the head.
Carefully cut all cranial and spinal nerves.
Remove the brain from the skull.
Fixate the brain/spinal cord in 20 mL of freshly prepared 4% PFA for 8 h.
Wash the brain 3× in 0.1 M phosphate buffer.
Transfer the brain into glycerol and leave it for 8 h for clearing.
Mount the brain on depression slides with a coverslip above as preparation for confocal microscopy.
Mount the slide with the preparation onto the Mavig VivaScope RS-G4 for imaging.
Select a long working distance objective suitable for the thickness of the brain tissue, such as a 60× Olympus UPLSAPO60XO with NA 1.3 oil objective.
Scan the brain tissue in optical sections ranging from 0.5 to 1 μm thickness for different wavelengths.
Free the deeply anesthetized tadpole from mechanical fixation after injection of microalgae.
Decapitate the animal with a small scissor at the level of the upper spinal cord.
Remove the lower jaws and visceral organs with the same scissor.
Pin the skull with the dorsal side up onto the Sylgard floor with minutiae.
Remove the skin on the skull with fine forceps and a microscissor.
Open the skull at the rostral end and remove the cartilaginous tissue above the brain until the decapitated end of the head.
Identify and cut the ocular motor nerve that supplies the superior rectus eye muscle at its innervation site at the target muscle with a microscissor.
Free the nerve from connective tissue.
Leave the preparation in the frog Ringer solution at 16°C–17°C in darkness for at least two hours to ensure full recovery of neuronal tissue.
Calibrate O2 electrodes using a 0 μmol · L-1 O2 solution (prepared with 0.1 M · L-1 ascorbic acid in 0.1 M · L-1 NaOH).
Calibrate O2 electrodes using a 270 μmol · L-1 O2 solution (air saturated Ringer solution).
Calibrate O2 electrodes using a 1,350 μmol · L-1 O2 solution (carbogen saturated Ringer solution).
Mount the recording chamber onto a metal support plate underneath a binocular with a zoomable lens.
Place and fix the tip of a fiber thermometer in one corner of the recording chamber.
Connect the inflow of the recording chamber to an antechamber dedicated for oxygen level adjustment.
Connect the inflow of the antechamber with a 1-liter bottle of frog Ringer solution placed at an elevated position.
Lead the connecting tube through a flow meter and a box with crushed ice to cool the Ringer solution.
Mount a tripod with a 3-axes micromanipulator onto the metal base plate.
Place an electrode holder equipped with a connector for a polyethylene tube onto the micromanipulator.
Attach a polyethylene tube (Inner diameter: 2 mm) to the connector of the electrode holder.
Connect the other end of the polyethylene tube to a 5 mL syringe.
Attach a wire from the electrode holder to an amplifier (EXT 10-2F; npi electronics; Tamm, Germany).
Mount two O2-sensitive microsensors with tip diameters of 10 μm onto a piezo-stepper attached to a micromanipulator.
Connect the output of the O2-sensitive microsensors and the amplifier to an A/D board (CED 1401, Cambridge Electronic Design, UK).
Digitize O2 concentration recordings and concurrent spike activity at 120 Hz and 5 kHz, respectively.
Store digitized data on a computer for offline analysis.
Mount a vertical bar with a clamp onto the metal base plate.
Fix a light source at a distance of 5 cm above the recording chamber.
Set the light intensity to 100 μE.
Ensure that the flow of Ringer solution produces a temperature of 17°C inside the recording chamber.
Maintain a sufficient level of frog Ringer solution in the chamber.
Place the isolated preparation in the center of the recording chamber.
Secure the preparation using minutiae (0.2 mm).
Position a freshly calibrated O2-sensitive microsensor inside the IVth ventricle using a micromanipulator.
Target the small opening between the caudal end of the cerebellum and the rostral end of the choroid plexus.
Place a second freshly calibrated O2-sensitive microsensor next to the preparation in the recording chamber, at 2 mm distance and same dorso-ventral level below the Ringer surface.
Pull electrodes from borosilicate glass using a P-87 Brown/Flaming electrode puller.
Break the tip of each electrode to fit the diameter of the superior oblique motor nerve.
Place the tip of the recording electrode with a micromanipulator at the distal end of the transected superior oblique motor nerve.
Gently pull the nerve into the electrode by providing negative pressure with a 5 mL syringe.
Ensure the nerve tightly fills and remains mechanically stable within the electrode tip.
Move the electrode with the micromanipulator to avoid stretching the nerve.
Let the preparation recover in darkness for 30 min.
